name: Great Plains
label: Homestead
lede: Ron House fronted a Columbus band that wrote about Rutherford B. Hayes, Lincoln Logs and record-store clerks, and put it all out on Homestead, a label with a name for unpaid royalties.

eras.title: Columbus, two years before a record
eras.text: House had already been through Moses Carryout, Twisted Shouts and Ron & the True Believers. In 1981 he starts a band with two brothers and a drummer, then spends two years turning it into Great Plains.

years.src: Wikipedia: Ron House · Grokipedia: Great Plains
years.h: [[Ron House|f6375d7a-1ad5-4ae6-a86b-6fcfcd9763c0]] and the Wyatt brothers start a band in Columbus
years.p: Matt Wyatt plays guitar, Mark Wyatt organ, Dave Green drums, and Don Howland, who goes by Hank O'Hare, bass.
years.xp:
House came to Columbus from Wooster to attend Ohio State. Great Plains was the first of his bands to stick.

Grokipedia credits Howland on bass from 1981 to 1983 and lists Mike Hummel, Paul Nini and Jim Castoe as the bassists who followed. It says Green went by "Manic."

years.cap: Flyer for Violent Femmes and Great Plains at Mr. Brown's Descent, Columbus, July 7, 1983
years.src: Wikipedia: Great Plains (Ohio band) · Trouser Press: Great Plains · The American Prospect: Big Wind From Ohio · Columbus Memory: Violent Femmes flyer
years.h: Great Plains' first record is an eight-song EP on New Age
years.p: The Mark, Don & Mel arrives before Homestead does. On July 7, 1983 the band shares a Columbus bill with the Violent Femmes at Mr. Brown's Descent.
years.xp:
Trouser Press titles it The Mark, Don & Me!. The band's own Bandcamp reissue calls it "Mark, Don & Mel." The American Prospect names "Pretty Dictionary" among its songs.

Matt Wyatt later told the magazine the early sessions happened in a studio where commercial jingles were the norm, and the band was "shuttled off into our little booths."

eras.title: Homestead takes them in
eras.text: Homestead, a Long Island sublabel run by Gerard Cosloy, puts out the first two Great Plains LPs. The history-nerd songwriting arrives with them.

years.cap: Flyer for a Great Plains in-store at Schoolkids Records, Columbus, 1984
years.src: Robert Christgau: Great Plains · Wikipedia: Homestead Records · Bandcamp Daily: How Homestead Records · Columbus Memory: Schoolkids flyer
years.h: Homestead puts out Born in a Barn
years.p: The first Great Plains LP gets a B+ from Robert Christgau, who notes that each folk-punk arrangement stands apart.
years.xp:
Homestead began in 1983 as a sublabel of the Long Island distributor Dutch East India Trading. Founder Sam Berger left in 1984 and Gerard Cosloy, who had made the fanzine Conflict, became its sole employee.

Bandcamp Daily counts Great Plains among Homestead's initial roster. Wikipedia adds the label's reputation: poor communication with artists, and unpaid royalties.

The flyer for the Schoolkids Records in-store, on High St. in Columbus, pitches the new LP Born in a Barn.

years.cap: The Offense newsletter no. 55, Columbus, March 22, 1985, with a Great Plains feature
years.src: Vice: Straight to Vinyl, Finally · Bandcamp Daily: How Homestead Records · Robert Christgau: Great Plains · Trouser Press: Great Plains · The American Prospect: Big Wind From Ohio · Columbus Memory: The Offense no. 55
years.h: Naked at the Buy, Sell and Trade puts the record-store clerk in a song
years.p: "Letter to a Fanzine" needles indie-shop clerks and the labels they pledge loyalty to. Bandcamp Daily and Vice both single it out.
years.xp:
Vice calls "Letter to a Fanzine" one of the best meta-commentaries on the underground. Bandcamp Daily describes a needling guitar hook over washes of organ. Christgau gave the album a B+ and called its organ-driven songs "objectively boring" and hummable anyway.

The American Prospect adds "Dick Clark," a song about rock's commercialism, from the same record.

Dates disagree. Wikipedia and Trouser Press say 1985; Christgau, the Prospect and the band's own Bandcamp say 1986.

Columbus had its own fanzine coverage. The newsletter The Offense ran a Great Plains feature and a band photo in its March 22, 1985 issue.
play: Naked at the Buy, Sell and Trade

years.big: "The trajectory of a set really depended on Ron's blood-alcohol level."
years.src: The American Prospect: Big Wind From Ohio
years.h: A Pittsburgh tape that beats the studio versions
years.p: Mark Wyatt on how a Great Plains show went. A recording from the Electric Banana on May 22, 1985 survives, and the American Prospect says it tops several of the studio takes.
years.xp:
The Prospect has the band calling its shows a high-wire act. Wyatt added that set lists were hastily written down and then often discarded.

The tape is titled Live at the Electric Banana, Pittsburgh 5.22.85. Great Plains also played a 1985 set at Staches in Columbus that was filmed.

years.cap: Great Plains at Stache's, Columbus, August 9, 1985
years.src: Furious: Thomas Jefferson Slave Apartments interview · Columbus Memory: Great Plains at Stache's
years.h: Great Plains share a Stache's stage with the Replacements
years.p: The poster for August 9, 1985 puts the Replacements and Great Plains on one Columbus bill. House also names the Replacements as a band he played with in these years.
years.xp:
In the Furious interview House says that around 1982 "things were returning to sort of an anti-English thing, more of an American roots thing," and names the [[The Embarrassment|487904ff-d3ef-477e-813a-c27548bc0570]] and the Gun Club as reference points.

On the Replacements, he said they "got worse around then and you only had the Pixies and Sonic Youth otherwise."

eras.title: American history, plugged in
eras.text: House reads Edmund Wilson's Civil War book and starts writing about presidents, ballplayers and Serpent Mound. The band gets louder, and critics split on whether that helped.

years.src: The American Prospect: Big Wind From Ohio · Erasing Clouds: Great Plains
years.h: Hayes, Lincoln Logs and the Black Sox land in House's songs
years.p: House's reading in Edmund Wilson's Patriotic Gore and 19th-century Ohio politics turns up in "Rutherford B. Hayes," "Lincoln Logs" and "Black Sox Scandal."
years.xp:
The American Prospect lists "Dick Clark," "Black Like Me," "Origin of My Silly Grin" and "Serpent Mound" alongside them. It credits House's reading in Wilson, post-structuralism and Ohio political history.

Reviewer Dave Heaton later heard dirty punk rock "in the Ohio sense," with new wave melody. The Comfest set above includes "Lincoln Logs" and "Serpent Mound."

years.cap: Dave Green, Mark Wyatt, Ron House, Paul Nini and Matt Wyatt, Columbus
years.src: Robert Christgau: Great Plains · Trouser Press: Great Plains · Wikipedia: Great Plains (Ohio band) · Columbus Memory: Great Plains portrait
years.h: Christgau grades Sum Things Up an A−, his best for them
years.p: He compares House to Tom Waits and tells readers to catch the band live.
years.xp:
Trouser Press reviewer Ira Robbins thought the later records suffered from overproduction and louder arrangements. Christgau disagreed and praised House's literary ambitions.

Wikipedia and Trouser Press date the LP 1987; the band's Bandcamp says 1988. A Before We Stop to Think EP is also dated 1987.

eras.title: The fun runs out
eras.text: By the end of the decade, House says, the shows weren't fun and Homestead had lost interest. The band ends in 1989.

years.cap: Flyer for Great Plains at Apollo's, Columbus, written by Ron House as a public apology
q: I noticed that the momentum had gone.
years.src: Furious: Thomas Jefferson Slave Apartments interview · Bandcamp Daily: How Homestead Records · Columbus Memory: Apollo's flyer
years.h: Eight years in, the shows stop being fun
years.p: "The shows just weren't that fun," House told Furious. He was ready to give up music, and Homestead cared less than it had in '85.
years.xp: He also said, "We never really got to be that famous." Gerard Cosloy, who signed the band, resigned from Homestead in 1990 and went on to co-found Matador.

years.p: Wikipedia lists the 1989 collection among the band's last releases.

eras.title: Uncaring on purpose
eras.text: House starts a new band meant to ignore what anyone thinks, and ends up on a major label anyway.

years.src: Furious: Thomas Jefferson Slave Apartments interview · Wikipedia: Thomas Jefferson Slave Apartments
years.h: House starts Thomas Jefferson Slave Apartments and stops caring who's listening
years.p: The idea, House told Furious, was to get drunk and not worry about what everyone else said.
years.xp:
Wikipedia dates the band to 1989, with guitarist Bob Petric among the core members. The name refers to Thomas Jefferson's slave quarters at Monticello.

House told Furious he thought he had "run that whole 'angry punk' thing into the ground."

years.src: Wikipedia: Thomas Jefferson Slave Apartments · Robert Christgau: Great Plains · The American Prospect: Big Wind From Ohio
years.h: An $800 record gets House onto American Recordings
years.p: Bait and Switch by Thomas Jefferson Slave Apartments comes out via Onion Records and American Recordings.
years.xp:
Wikipedia says it was recorded for $800. Christgau gave it an A− and said the opening songs rush by in a perfect furious tunefest.

The American Prospect calls the band more commercially successful than Great Plains had been.

eras.title: The catalog comes back
eras.text: Old 3C Records, run by a former Great Plains bassist, reissues the Homestead-era work, and the songs go online in full.

years.src: Robert Christgau: Length of Growth · Erasing Clouds: Great Plains · The American Prospect: Big Wind From Ohio
years.h: Old 3C Records gathers it all as Length of Growth 1981-89
years.p: Fifty songs on two discs, with a B+ from Christgau and his candid note that not all of it is great and some is barely good.
years.xp:
Old 3C Records issued it. The American Prospect dates it 2000; Wikipedia and Christgau say 2001. The Prospect follows it with Cornflakes (2003), an odds and ends collection, and says Old 3C was run by a former Great Plains bassist.

Wikipedia names that bassist Paul Nini; the Prospect calls him Paul Wyatt.

years.p: It comes out on Moses Carryout Records, his own label. During the 1990s he'd also become part owner of Columbus's Used Kids record store.

years.cap: Ron House at Southpaw, Brooklyn, April 25, 2008
years.h: Great Plains play "Letter to a Fanzine" on WFMU's Cherry Blossom Clinic
years.p: The set is on WFMU's Cherry Blossom Clinic, 8/22/2008, and the Free Music Archive lists the recording.

years.h: House and Times New Viking's Jared Phillips record as Counter Intuits
years.p: Sheets of Hits (2013) and Monosyllabilly (2016) come out on House's Pyramid Scheme imprint.

years.src: Great Plains Bandcamp: Length of Growth 1981-89 (vol. 1) · Great Plains Bandcamp: Length of Growth 1981-89 (vol. 2)
years.h: Both volumes of Length of Growth go up on Bandcamp
years.p: Released August 5, 2020: 24 tracks on vol. 1, 27 on vol. 2.
